sections.title: Loss-on-Drying and Switch-Off Criteria Explained
sections.tabSummary: How HE53 decides when a sample is dry
body: How HE53 actually decides when a sample has finished drying, rather than just running a fixed timer.

Loss-on-drying moisture testing works by heating a sample and tracking how much weight it loses as moisture evaporates, but knowing when to stop matters as much as the heating itself. Stop too early and the reading understates moisture content; run too long and the result can drift as the sample begins to degrade rather than simply dry.

HE53's automatic switch-off (SOC 3) monitors the rate of weight loss and ends the test once the sample has genuinely stopped losing moisture, rather than running to a fixed time regardless of the sample. A timed switch-off is also available for sample types where a fixed drying duration is the better fit.

rows: Stopping before the sample has actually finished drying
Ending the test based on actual weight-loss rate
Running longer than needed on a fast-drying sample
A result tied to genuine moisture loss, not a guessed duration
Inconsistent endpoints across different sample types
A consistent, sample-driven stopping point
No flexibility when a fixed duration IS the better fit
A timed option still available where it's genuinely needed

sections.tabSummary: What guided setup and live visibility actually remove from method development
body: What guided method setup and live drying visibility actually remove from testing a new sample type.

Setting up a moisture test correctly, choosing the right temperature, drying program, and switch-off criteria for a given sample, normally depends on the operator's experience with that specific material, and getting it wrong means either an inaccurate result or wasted time re-running the test. That's a bigger problem in a lab handling many different sample types than in one running the same method every day.

HC103's Method Wizard walks the operator through parameter selection step by step, and the Temperature Assistant helps identify the right drying temperature for materials the operator hasn't tested before. Once a test is running, the real-time drying curve on the touchscreen shows exactly how the sample is losing weight over time, so an unusual drying pattern is visible as it happens, not just in the final result.

rows: Wrong parameters on an unfamiliar sample type

Live tracking of exactly how the sample is drying

sections.tabSummary: What result prediction and a full audit trail actually add to a busy lab
body: What result prediction and a full audit trail actually add to a lab running many samples a day.

A full loss-on-drying test takes time, however fast the drying program, and a lab waiting on that result before deciding the next step loses that time every single run. HX204's QuickPredict™ analyzes the drying curve as it develops and estimates the final moisture value before the test physically finishes, giving an early, reliable read without cutting the actual test short.

The same lab that benefits from a faster read usually also has to prove every result later. HX204's full 21 CFR Part 11 compliance, control charts, and automatic centralized result collection with LabX mean every test is captured, timestamped, and tied to an auditable record from the moment it runs, not reconstructed from a printout afterward.

sections.tabSummary: What real multi-operator governance and trend tracking add to a shared instrument
body: What real multi-operator governance and long-term trend tracking add to an instrument multiple people rely on.

A moisture analyzer shared across a shift, or across a whole lab, faces two risks a single-operator instrument doesn't: someone changing a setting they shouldn't, and no one noticing a slow drift in performance until a result finally looks wrong. Neither is a single bad reading, both are slower, harder-to-catch problems.

HS153's 10 customizable user groups and up to 30 user profiles let a lab define exactly who can access what, backed by auto-lock and password protection. Control charts address the second problem directly, plotting instrument performance over time so drift shows up as a trend on a chart, not as a surprise result months later.
